items.passage: Fifteen years, two languages, one rule: an interpreter carries what is said, not what is meant. That rule brought me, Benedita, to the edge of a dirt soccer field on the plateau at dusk, beside Nova, a scout who had flown from Lisbon to meet the coach known across the region as a finder of talent. Nova had questions about drills and formations. The coach answered about roads. For twenty years, he said, he had driven the school van three hours each way on Saturdays to sheep camps without a road of their own, and he had never lost a player to distance. I put each sentence into Portuguese exactly; for once, what he said and what he meant were the same. Nova's pen stayed capped. When the light failed, the coach parked the van at the touchline and switched on its headlights, and the boys played on inside the two long beams, their shadows running ahead of them.

options: A scout travels far to learn a celebrated coach's drills and formations for young players.
An interpreter's duty is to carry exactly what is said, setting aside what the speaker means.

Rory has a glue for such repairs, made from a recipe he has never written down; for three years you have asked for it and been told you will learn it when you need it. He mixes it now while you watch, measuring nothing, talking about the weather. When you reach for a pencil, he sends you to the shed for clamps. Next morning he announces that his wrists are bad and the second batch is yours. You ruin it twice. On the third try he leans on the bench beside you, his wrists apparently healed, and tilts the pot a quarter-turn toward the window.

items.passage: What is owed to someone who leaves without a word and returns the same way? I turned that over at the bus depot in Gdansk, where my brother Marcus and I waited for our cousin Zofia, eleven years after she had boarded a night coach to Berlin. Marcus had polished his shoes and rehearsed, in the van, how the radio shop could use another pair of hands. I had rehearsed something sharper. She stepped down with one small bag, thinner than I remembered, kissed us both, and explained nothing. On the drive home she asked about every customer she could still name. I noticed that she flinched when the van door slammed and kept her bag on her knees the whole way. I did not say the sharp thing. At the depot behind us, a cleaner pushed a wide broom across bays stained with oil.

items.passage: Night makes people truthful. At the sanatorium above the lake outside Bergen, I was the nurse who sat up with the patients who could not sleep, and Thorvald was the most stubborn of them. He would not lie down until I wheeled him to the end of the dock, where he watched the water as if a boat were due. On the fourth night he told me about his brother, a quarrel over their father's boathouse, and a letter he had written the week after and carried in his coat ever since. His brother had died the following spring. I said that someone in the family might still read the letter, and he shook his head. An apology, he said, was a door that opens from one side only. After that he spoke less and slept more. When he asked me, Sigrid, to burn the envelope in the ward stove, I did, and I noticed that he no longer looked out at the water.
items.question: As used in the text, the phrase “a door that opens from one side only” most nearly suggests that an apology is
options: a gesture Thorvald could make only after his brother first forgave him
a private confession that should stay hidden from everyone, even Sigrid
an act Thorvald had refused to begin because of his stubborn pride
an offering that needs someone living on the other side to receive it

items.passage:
Who pays a clockmaker for the hours he gives away?
On Forty-Third Street my father, Santiago,
kept every clock in the window five minutes fast
so passersby would think themselves late and hurry in.
Ottavio came in January with his wife's watch,
mainspring snapped, the crystal fogged like breath on glass.
He laid his nickels out in a careful row.
My father slid them back across the counter
and bent above the bench past closing, past supper,
lending the stranger his own evening,
asking nothing on account.
I translated nothing. Nothing needed saying.
When the small heart started, Ottavio wept in Italian;
my father answered him in Spanish.
Neither man asked when the debt would come due.
I stood between them holding my English,
the one who believed words were the price of things.
items.question: As used in the text, the phrase “lending the stranger his own evening” most nearly suggests that Santiago was
options: giving up his own time without expecting anything in return
advancing his time to Ottavio on the promise of later payment
sacrificing family hours out of a shopkeeper's sense of duty
stretching the repair slowly to make the evening feel longer

items.passage:
Once the library on Central Avenue was ours,
its radiators ticking like patient clocks,
Elan at the window with the paper folded small
while I, Nayeli, wandered the stacks.
We had a system: I chose, he signed,
and neither of us called it trust.
One Saturday in March, between the atlases,
he mentioned that the house was sold,
Denver by June, the papers settled.
Settled, I said, admiring the word
the way one admires a stranger's handwriting.
Now I notice that the radiators hiss.
I notice how the books lean on one another
like people who have never been introduced.
I check out a road map, sign for it myself,
and practice the signature until it looks like someone older.
items.question: Which choice best describes the shift in tone that occurs in the poem?
options: From restless impatience to quiet acceptance of the planned move
From warm gratitude to open, tearful pleading with Elan to stay
From affectionate ease to guarded irony after the news
From shy uncertainty to growing excitement about a new life in Denver

items.passage: By the seventh evening of the rains, the people of the lane had made a song about Kwesi. Up the stairs he went to Obinna's projection booth, always with the same cracked lens bundled in a cloth, and down he came with the lens glued and the song a verse longer. Obinna, who mended everything in the old Accra cinema, from ceiling fans to torn reels, played his part well. He sighed loudly, rolled his eyes for the children watching from the steps, and glued. Glass is like a promise, he told them; mend it once and it remembers the break. On the seventh evening, though, he raised the lens into the projector's beam to test his work, and the picture on the screen below came apart into two faces, one bright and one faint. Obinna lowered the lens. The children on the steps stopped singing without being told. In a voice the lane had never heard him use, he asked Kwesi whose film had last passed through this glass, and when Kwesi answered, Obinna wrapped the lens in his own handkerchief.
items.question: Which choice best describes the shift in tone in the text?
options: From playful, communal teasing to a hushed and reverent stillness
From weary irritation with Kwesi to sudden anger at his deception
From gentle mockery of Obinna to admiring praise of his great skill
From cheerful curiosity about the lens to anxious fear of its strange power

items.passage: We found the letters in a biscuit tin under the workbench of our mother's radio shop in Marrakesh, a week after the funeral. Yiannis read them aloud while I, Yasmin, sorted vacuum tubes into egg cartons. Each was from a man who signed with a single initial, thanking her for another repair she had refused to charge for, month after month, for eleven years. My brother set the last one down and looked at me, and I knew the word he was not saying. __She had always closed the shop an hour early on Thursdays, and she had never once told us where she went.__ For a while neither of us spoke. Then Yiannis turned the tin over, and a pamphlet slid out from beneath the paper lining: a schedule of Thursday evening readings at a school for the blind, with our mother listed as the volunteer who kept its radios working. The same initial was printed beside the director's name. Outside, the call to prayer rose over the rooftops, and Yiannis began, very carefully, to put the letters back in order.

items.passage: On the first Tuesday of each month, I fetched my younger brother Wolfram from a reading room near the Ringstrasse in Vienna, where his tutor, Anselm, taught him geography from maps older than our grandparents. Anselm was always late, he hummed while he corrected, and he would not let Wolfram use the tram diagram I had copied out for him. A boy should know a city by its faces, he said, its domes and fountains and shop signs, not by its numbered lines. I told my mother this was an old man's vanity. In February the trams stopped for two days in a snowstorm, and I went out in a panic and found Wolfram already halfway home, steering past the green church dome, the bakery's brass pretzel, the fountain with the chipped nose. I said nothing to Anselm about it the next Tuesday. He was late again, and humming. But I waited for him in the reading room instead of the cold hall, and on the walk home I let Wolfram choose the way.
items.question: Which choice best describes the narrator's attitude toward Anselm?
options: Lasting suspicion, since she still doubts that his methods kept Wolfram safe
Open gratitude, since she thanks him warmly for preparing Wolfram so well
Grudging respect, shown more in her actions than in anything she tells him
Weary tolerance, since his lateness and humming still outweigh his lessons

items.passage: Who should stay behind when the olives go down to market? So begin the tellers on the terraces above Naples, and so began young Emilio, newly sent to the hill school, who answered the question with great confidence. The slowest reader, he declared, would stay to mind the trees. Alessia read slowly and counted faster than the priest. She folded her arms and stayed. By noon the baskets at market were tallied wrong, the prices tangled, and Emilio was climbing back up the hill with his collar undone, a climb the tellers describe at length and with evident pleasure. They are careful to add that he asked Alessia's pardon before he asked her help, and that the following year he chose by drawing lots. Some insist he never admitted the error aloud; others say he admitted it only to the trees. Grandmothers telling it still pause here to slice the bread.

options: Stern disapproval, presenting his decision as a lasting stain on the school

items.passage: On the Thursday after the funeral, Josiah carried his late teacher's violin into the laundromat because he had nowhere else to wait while his shirts dried. Harriet, who conducted the youth orchestra, was folding towels two machines away. Everyone had assumed the old man would leave the instrument to her, his oldest student, not to a fourteen-year-old who still rushed his scales. Josiah offered to give it to her. Harriet looked at the dented case, then asked him to play something. She listened through two cycles of the dryers without correcting a note, and afterward she wrote down the name of a shop that restrings old violins cheaply. Outside, a bus hissed at the curb, and steam from the vents curled into the cold air.

He told me to hold one end of the chain steady, Putri, steady, and while he worked the links he described a sandal he had torn as a boy and the stray dog he had blamed for it. items.passage: Oaxaca was dry that March, and the river below my grandmother's village had shrunk to stones and cracked mud. Halfway across, Esperanza stopped and asked me to say my whole name. I said Eulalio, the name on my school papers. She waited, so I added the second one, which my parents had written on my birth record and never used. She asked me to say it again, louder, and then again. Years later I learned it had been her younger brother's, lost at this crossing in a high-water season, and that she was the last in the village who still spoke it. That afternoon, though, I only felt foolish shouting at stones. On the far bank a boy sold cold tamarind drinks from a cooler, and we each bought one.

"Translate only what I say," Somchai told me the first morning, and so I have, Mother, for six weeks in this printing room in Chiang Mai. Yesterday the investors asked who had designed the new press. Somchai glanced at the young mechanic oiling the rollers and said the design was his own. I had seen the mechanic's drawings pinned above his bench, and for a moment I nearly said so. Then I remembered that on my first day the same investors had asked which workers came from families who owed them money, and that the mechanic had gone pale and left the room. I translated Somchai's claim word for word. My face burned the whole afternoon. This morning the presses started early, and the room smells of ink and wet paper. Please send the recipe for the mango rice.

Mai

items.passage: I, Faris, found the letters on our third day snowed into the cabin above Beirut, tucked under the lining of my grandfather's desk drawer. Every one was addressed to Noor, his oldest friend, who was waiting out the storm with us, and none had been sent. In them he admitted that a prize-winning poem from their student years had been hers, not his. Noor sat knitting by the stove. Twice that week I had heard her remark that my grandfather never once apologized for anything, and both times she laughed as if it did not matter.
